text:
Help me write a public comment. I run a charter fishing boat out of our harbor, and the state fish and wildlife commission is taking comment on cutting the daily summer flounder limit from 4 fish per angler to 2.

Facts:
- I've run my boat for 22 years. I take out about 160 trips a season at $900 a trip for up to 6 people.
- There are 11 charter boats in our harbor.
- In a survey our charter association ran, 41 of 70 past customers said they would book fewer trips if the limit drops to 2. 12 said they'd book the same number.
- The commission staff's report says the flounder stock is at 78% of its target and recommends the cut for 3 years.
- Charter boats land about 9% of the state's summer flounder. Private boats land about 80%.
- The last time the limit was cut, in 2016, my bookings dropped from 170 trips to 138 the next season and came back to 155 two years later.

I want to say this limit will put every charter boat in our harbor out of business. I get two minutes at the microphone.

Before I draft, there's one problem to raise. Then I have a few questions.

**The "every boat goes out of business" claim.** Your own numbers work against it. In 2016 your bookings fell from 170 trips to 138, about 19%, and came back to 155 within two years. You stayed in business. If a commissioner or staff member points that out, the rest of your two minutes loses credibility. My recommendation is to say what the cut actually costs. In 2016, 32 lost trips at $900 came to $28,800 for one boat. Multiply that across 11 boats and say it in dollars and jobs. Then make one firm point: charter boats land 9% of the catch, so cutting their limit does little for the stock. That's an argument staff can't easily wave off.

These answers would change the piece:

1. **What exactly do you want the commission to do?** Your options include keeping 4 fish, a compromise at 3, a shorter period than 3 years, or a separate limit for for-hire boats. A clear ask gets more traction than a plain "no."
2. **Is this time different from 2016, and can you show it?** Examples would be higher fuel, insurance or slip costs, or thinner margins. If losing around 30 trips would actually push you below break-even, tell me roughly where that line is. That's the only way an "out of business" claim holds up.
3. **Did any boats in your harbor close or sell after the 2016 cut?** If so, how many?
4. **Who else depends on your trips?** Crew you employ, plus local businesses like bait shops, fuel docks, restaurants and motels. Rough numbers are fine.
5. **How was the survey run?** How were the 70 customers chosen, and what did the other 17 say? Someone may ask whether the sample was fair.

If you don't know some of these, that's fine. I'll leave them out and won't guess.

On the "every boat" line: I hear you. I still want it as strong as it can be, but not saying anything false. And I can't say how many boats would close. I only know my own books.

1. We'd accept 3 fish, or a shorter season, instead of 2.
2. I don't know. I can't say where my break-even is.
3. I don't know.
4. I don't know.
5. I don't know how they were picked or what the other 17 said.

<final_document>
Good evening. My name is [NAME]. I've run a charter boat out of [HARBOR] for 22 years, one of 11 charter boats there.

I'm not here to say the flounder don't need help. Your staff says the stock is at 78% of its target, and I believe them. Nobody needs those fish more than I do. I'm here to ask you to take the cut in a way that doesn't fall so hard on the boats that land the least.

Charter boats land about 9% of this state's summer flounder. Private boats land about 80%. Most of the fish this cut saves will come from private boats. For us, the cut comes out of our livelihood.

I can only speak for my own books, so here they are. When you cut the limit in 2016, my bookings fell from 170 trips to 138 the next season. That's 32 trips at $900 each, or $28,800 gone in one year. Two years later I was back up to 155, and I still hadn't reached where I started. That was one cut. This one runs three years.

Our charter association asked 70 past customers what they would do if the limit drops to 2. Forty-one said they would book fewer trips. Twelve said they'd book the same. People don't pay $900 for a day on the water to bring home two fish.

So I'm asking you for a middle path. Set the limit at 3 fish, or keep 4 with a shorter season. Either one still protects the stock, and either one gives boats like mine a fighting chance to get through the next three years.

Thank you.
</final_document>

Some notes on the draft:

- **Length:** about 290 words, which comes to roughly two minutes at a calm speaking pace. Read it aloud with a timer once. If you run long, cut the survey paragraph first.
- **The "every boat" line:** I kept it out. You can't back it up, and you don't need it. "I can only speak for my own books" followed by your real 2016 numbers is harder to argue with than a prediction, and nothing in it can be challenged.
- **"Shorter season":** I read this as keeping 4 fish with fewer open days. If you meant cutting to 2 fish but for fewer than 3 years, change the ask to "or keep the cut to one year instead of three."
- **The survey:** I gave your association's numbers as they are and made no claims about how customers were picked. If someone asks about the method, just say it was a survey of past customers and you don't have more detail.
